subject: physics
question_text: Derive the relation between the acceleration due to gravity g at the surface of a planet and the universal gravitational constant G.

verification.note: The mark split is invented and is a CLAIM until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it. The question itself is sourced, not invented.

recall_prompt: Say the steps you would write for this answer, in order. You can speak in English, in Telugu, or in both.

steps.label: The gravitational force
lines: Let a body of mass m rest on the surface of a
planet of mass M and radius R. By the law of
gravitation the planet pulls it with a force
steps.why: A sphere pulls an outside body exactly as though its whole mass sat at its centre, which is why R is the distance to use.
common_mistakes: Using the distance from the surface rather than the radius R from the centre.

recall.must_convey: That the gravitational force on the body is G M m by R squared.
accept: G M m by R squared
reject: that same force is the weight

steps.memory_tip: A sphere pulls as if all its mass sat at the centre — that is why the distance is R.
steps.margin_note: First mark. F = GMm/R², with R measured from the centre of the planet.

steps.label: The weight
lines: That same pull is what we call the weight of
the body, and weight is mass times the
steps.why: Naming the SAME force twice is the entire derivation; the algebra afterwards is one cancellation.
common_mistakes: Treating the gravitational pull and the weight as two different forces that must be added.

recall.must_convey: That the same force is the weight of the body, equal to m g.
accept: the same force is the weight
reject: G M m by R squared

steps.memory_tip: Name the SAME force twice: once as GMm/R², once as mg.
steps.margin_note: Second mark. One line: the same pull written again as mg.

steps.label: The relation
lines: Both expressions describe the same force, so

lines.text: m g = G M m / R²

lines: g depends only on the mass and radius of the
planet, never on the body placed on it.
steps.why: Because m cancels, every body falls with the same acceleration — the fact Galileo is remembered for.
common_mistakes: Keeping m in the final answer, which would make heavy bodies fall faster.

recall.must_convey: That m cancels, giving g equals G M by R squared, independent of the body.
accept: g equals G M by R squared

steps.memory_tip: Equate and cancel m: g = GM/R². The cancelled m is why every body falls alike.
steps.margin_note: The last two marks. Equate, cancel m, then box g = GM/R².

insider_note: Two of the four marks sit in the equating and the cancelling — writing g = GM/R² straight down earns the box and loses the working.
